definition: Requiring great care, effort, and precision because the standards are very high.
example: Translating poetry is exacting work, since every word choice changes the rhythm of a line.
nuance: Exacting stresses strict standards that call for precision, while demanding can simply mean tiring or needing lots of effort.
prompt: A veteran watchmaker is training a new apprentice in the workshop.
options: The exacting watchmaker made the apprentice redo any gear that was off by a hair.
The exacting watchmaker shrugged and told the apprentice that any rough fit would do.
The apprentice showed up at the exacting time of nine o'clock on his first morning.
Using thin tweezers, the exacting watchmaker pulled a dead battery from the case.
reasons: Refusing to accept even a tiny error shows the strict, precise standards the word describes.
Accepting sloppy work reflects low standards, the reverse of what the word means.
This confuses the word with exact; a time can be precise, but it cannot hold anyone to standards.
Pulling something out is extracting; the sentence shows a task, not high standards.

practice.prompt: A pastry chef is making a delicate caramel for a baking competition.
options: Taking an exacting approach, she tossed random handfuls of flour into the bowl without measuring.
The judges granted her the exacting number of minutes she had asked for at the start.
After the long contest she felt so exacting that she napped on the couch for hours.
The recipe was exacting, so she checked that the sugar reached precisely 240 degrees.
reasons: Careless guessing is the opposite of working to strict, precise standards.
This mistakes the word for exact; a number of minutes cannot be strict or demanding.
This confuses the word with exhausted; the word describes standards, not tiredness.
A recipe that leaves no room for error calls for careful, precise work.
